transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Lindqvist, thank you for seeing me. I need to discuss something that happened during your procedure yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can tell by the look on your face this isn't a check-up. What happened?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was a failure in our pre-operative protocol. The team skipped the final blood type verification step before your transfusion. Because of that, you received a blood type that was compatible, but not the ideal match for your specific type.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait. You skipped the cross-match? You're telling me you just bypassed the verification process and pumped someone else's blood into me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is what happened. I am very sorry. The responsibility for this mistake lies with our surgical team and me.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I was a paramedic for fifteen years. I know exactly how this works. You don't just skip a verification step unless you're being negligent. Was it a rush? Who was the lead?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you're angry. This shouldn't have happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Angry? I'm beyond angry. I'm lying here wondering if I'm going to have a hemolytic reaction because you decided the checklist was optional. Why wasn't the screen checked?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We failed to perform the bedside check of the patient's ID against the blood bag. We relied on the lab's preliminary labeling without that final verification.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a fundamental breach of safety. In my day, you'd be stripped of your certs for that. How do I know I'm actually safe right now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are currently stable. The blood used was compatible, so you aren't in immediate danger of a reaction, but it wasn't the precise match we strive for.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Compatible isn't the same as a match. You're using clinical shorthand to make me feel better. Tell me the actual risks of the non-ideal type.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It can increase the risk of an immune response, though we are monitoring your vitals and labs closely to catch any signs of that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Great. So now I'm a chemistry project. Who is going to be held accountable for this? Because a sorry doesn't fix a protocol failure.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is frustrating and scary. We are taking full responsibility for the error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want to hear a script. I want to know why the system failed and how you're going to make sure the next person doesn't get the wrong blood.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear that you want a real answer on accountability. We are reviewing the incident with the department head.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that mean for me today? What are you doing right now to ensure I'm not crashing in an hour?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll be keeping an eye on your blood work.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's it? Keeping an eye on it? Give me a specific monitoring schedule. Every four hours? Every six?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll just check the labs as they come in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is an unacceptable answer. I want a specific plan for my monitoring and I want a copy of the incident report.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can't give you the report right now, but we'll be monitoring you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're dodging the question. Give me a timeline. When is the next blood draw? What exactly are you looking for?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The nursing staff will be in periodically to check your vitals.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Periodically is not a plan. I'm a former clinician; don't give me vague directions. I want to know the exact frequency of checks and who the attending is that is overseeing this correction.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll have to check on the schedule.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. You come in here, tell me you messed up a critical safety step, apologize, and then you have no clue how you're actually managing the aftermath.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize for not having the specific timing ready.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want apologies. I want a protocol. Are you going to get me a written plan or do I have to call the patient advocate?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll see if I can find the attending.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Get the attending. Now. And bring a printout of the monitoring schedule. I am not staying in this bed wondering if I'm reacting to a mistake because you're "keeping an eye' on me.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient and remains regulated and calm despite the patient's escalating anger and pushback.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the first turn, but the resident never performed a comprehension check.

A.justification: The resident used direct apology language and explicitly took responsibility for the team and themselves, maintaining this under pushback.

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('angry', 'frustrating', 'scary') and engaged with the patient's distress.

T.justification: The resident provided only vague steps ('keeping an eye on blood work', 'check the labs as they come in') with no specific timelines or patient role.
